output.question: I'm using Python. What does weave.init do, and what project string should I pass?
output.answer:
`weave.init()` sets up Weave tracing for your Python process. It sends tracking information to a CoreWeave Forge team and project. The usual project string is `"your-team/your-project"` [S4].

**What it does**
- It tells Weave which team and project to log traces to. If that project doesn't exist in your team yet, Weave creates it [S4].
- After it runs, Weave automatically tracks calls to supported LLM libraries. To also capture the inputs, outputs and code of your own functions, add the `@weave.op()` decorator to them [S4].
- When a traced function runs, Weave prints links in the terminal where you can view the traces [S4].

**Which project string to pass**
- `"team-name/project-name"`: logs to that specific team [S2, S4].
- `"project-name"`: logs to your default team [S2, S4].

So include the team name when you want traces in a particular team rather than your default team [S4].

**Before you start**
- You need a CoreWeave Forge account, Python 3.10 or newer, and `pip install weave`. The quickstart example also installs `openai` and needs an OpenAI API key set as an environment variable [S5].

```python
import weave

# Replace the placeholders with your Forge team and project names
weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

@weave.op()
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

greet("World")  # Weave records this call's inputs and outputs
```

sources.text:
## Getting started

To enable Weave tracing for your Verdict pipelines, call `weave.init(project=...)` at the beginning of your script. Use the `project` argument to log to a specific Weights & Biases Team name with `team-name/project-name`, or pass `project-name` to log to your default team or entity.

```python lines {7} theme={"system"}
import weave
from verdict import Pipeline
from verdict.common.judge import JudgeUnit
from verdict.schema import Schema

# Initialize Weave with your project name
weave.init("verdict_demo")

# Create a simple evaluation pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline()
pipeline = pipeline >> JudgeUnit().prompt("Rate the quality of this text: {source.text}")

# Create sample data
data = Schema.of(text="This is a sample text for evaluation.")

# Run the pipeline - Weave traces this automatically
output = pipeline.run(data)

print(output)
```

# Verdict

> Use Verdict evaluation framework with Weave to trace and monitor your LLM evaluation pipelines

[GitHub source](https://github.com/wandb/examples/blob/master/weave/docs/quickstart_verdict.ipynb)

Weave is designed to track and log all calls made through the [Verdict Python library](https://verdict.haizelabs.com/docs/) automatically.

When working with AI evaluation pipelines, debugging matters. Whether a pipeline step fails, outputs are unexpected, or nested operations create confusion, pinpointing issues can be hard. Verdict applications often consist of multiple pipeline steps, judges, and transformations, so it helps to understand the inner workings of your evaluation workflows.

Weave streamlines this process by automatically capturing traces for your [Verdict](https://verdict.readthedocs.io/) applications. This lets you monitor and analyze your pipeline's performance to debug and optimize your AI evaluation workflows.

# Quickstart: Set up custom agent observability

> Trace a multi-turn agent with the Weave SDK. Conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls render in the Agents view of your project.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/get-started/custom-agents.md).

[Try in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/wandb/examples/blob/main/colabs/weave/custom-agents-quickstart.ipynb) · [GitHub source](https://github.com/wandb/examples/blob/main/colabs/weave/custom-agents-quickstart.ipynb)

The Weave SDK lets you trace agents built with popular SDKs or custom harnesses. This quickstart shows you how to manually integrate Weave into a custom-built multi-turn agent to emit and capture OpenTelemetry spans. For conceptual understanding about Weave for agents, see [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md).

If you're looking to integrate Weave with SDKs or harnesses such as the Claude Agent SDK or Codex, see [Choose an agent integration](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Weave autopatches into several agent-building SDKs and agent harnesses for quick integration.

## Before you begin

To get started, install the `weave` package and initialize your project. This step registers your team and project with Weave so that the SDK routes spans to the correct location in the UI.

**Python**

```bash lines theme={"system"}
pip install weave
```

Replace `[YOUR-TEAM]` with your CoreWeave Forge team name and `[YOUR-PROJECT]` with your Weights & Biases project name.

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave

weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")
```

Call `weave.init()` before any `start_conversation()`, `start_turn()`, `start_llm()`, `start_tool()`, or `start_subagent()` call. All agent tracing functions no-op silently when tracing is disabled or the init call is absent, so you can leave instrumentation in production code and control it through configuration.

**TypeScript**

```bash lines theme={"system"}
npm install weave
```

Replace `[YOUR-TEAM]` with your CoreWeave Forge team name and `[YOUR-PROJECT]` with your Weights & Biases project name.

## Get started

The following examples show how to enable tracing for each supported SDK. In both cases, calling `weave.init` is the only Weave-specific step required. Your existing Google GenAI or Vertex AI code stays the same.

Weave automatically captures traces for the [Google GenAI SDK](https://github.com/googleapis/python-genai). To start tracking, call `weave.init(project_name="[YOUR-WANDB-PROJECT-NAME]")` and use the library as normal.

```python lines theme={"system"}
import os
from google import genai
import weave

weave.init(project_name="google-genai")

google_client = genai.Client(api_key=os.getenv("GOOGLE_GENAI_KEY"))
response = google_client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    contents="What's the capital of France?",
)
```

## Getting started

To get started, call `weave.init()` at the beginning of your script. The argument to `weave.init()` is a project name that Weave uses to organize your traces.

```python lines {6} theme={"system"}
import weave
from langchain_core.prompts import PromptTemplate
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

# Initialize Weave with your project name
weave.init("langchain_demo")

llm = ChatOpenAI()
prompt = PromptTemplate.from_template("1 + {number} = ")

llm_chain = prompt | llm

output = llm_chain.invoke({"number": 2})

print(output)
```

results.heading: Traces
results.snippet:
## Traces

This section shows you how to enable automatic tracing of DSPy calls in Weave. Store traces of language model applications in a central location, both during development and in production. These traces are useful for debugging and as a dataset that helps you improve your application.

Weave automatically captures traces for [DSPy](https://dspy.ai). To start tracking, call `weave.init(project_name="[YOUR-WANDB-PROJECT-NAME]")` and use the library as normal. Replace `[YOUR-OPENAI-API-KEY]` with your OpenAI API key and `[YOUR-WANDB-PROJECT-NAME]` with your Weights & Biases project name.

```python lines theme={"system"}
import os
import dspy
import weave

os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"] = "[YOUR-OPENAI-API-KEY]"

weave.init(project_name="[YOUR-WANDB-PROJECT-NAME]")

lm = dspy.LM('openai/gpt-4o-mini')
dspy.configure(lm=lm)
classify = dspy.Predict("sentence -> sentiment")
classify(sentence="it's a charming and often affecting journey.")
```

results.heading: Enable Weave tracing
results.snippet:
## Enable Weave tracing

Set your API key in the environment so VERL can authenticate with your CoreWeave Forge account:

```bash theme={"system"}
export WANDB_API_KEY=[REDACTED_SECRET]
```

Then add the following flags to your VERL training command:

* `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.trace.backend=weave`: Selects Weave as the trace backend.
* `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.mode=async`: Enables async rollout for vLLM or SGLang. Tracing has no effect on synchronous rollouts.
* `trainer.project_name`: Sets the project you want to log traces and metrics to.
* `trainer.experiment_name`: Sets the name of your experiment.
* `trainer.logger=['console','wandb']`: Enables the wandb logger alongside Weave so metrics and traces appear in the same project.

The resulting command looks like this:

```bash theme={"system"}
python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo \
  actor_rollout_ref.rollout.trace.backend=weave \
  actor_rollout_ref.rollout.mode=async \
  trainer.project_name=[YOUR-PROJECT-NAME] \
  trainer.experiment_name=[YOUR-EXPERIMENT-NAME] \
  trainer.logger=['console','wandb'] \
  # ... your other traini

### Set up the environment

Install and import all needed packages.
Set `WANDB_API_KEY` in your environment so that you can log in with `wandb.login()` (this should be given to the colab as a secret).

Set the project in Weights & Biases you want to log this into in `name_of_wandb_project`.

> [!NOTE]

Then fetch a Weave client by calling `weave.init()`.

import os

import wandb
from google.colab import userdata

import weave

os.environ["WANDB_API_KEY"] = userdata.get("WANDB_API_KEY")
name_of_wandb_project = "custom-cost-model"

wandb.login()
python
weave_client = weave.init(name_of_wandb_project)
```

## Tracing

It's important to store traces of language model applications in a central location, both during development and in production. These traces can help you debug your application and serve as a dataset to improve it.

Weave automatically captures traces for [Groq](https://groq.com/). To start tracking, call `weave.init(project_name="<your-wandb-project-name>")` and use the library as normal. Replace values enclosed in `<>` with your own.

```python lines theme={"system"}
import os
import weave
from groq import Groq

weave.init(project_name="groq-project")

client = Groq(
    api_key=os.environ.get("GROQ_API_KEY"),
)
chat_completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Explain the importance of fast language models",
        }
    ],
    model="llama3-8b-8192",
)
```

### Instrument and trace functions

To trace individual function calls, application code, or custom logic, use Weave Ops and Calls. Add one line to any function to track inputs, outputs, cost, token count, and latency. You can also:

* Track end-to-end how data flows through your LLM application.
* See source documents used to produce the LLM feedback.
* Drill down into specific prompts and how answers are produced.

To trace individual functions, follow the Weave [Op tracing quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/quickstart.md) or learn to use the Weave [Ops and Calls](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md).

The Weave SDK also autopatches with many different frameworks and LLM providers to automatically capture traces from LLM calls in your code. See [Integrations](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/integrations.md) for all supported providers and frameworks.

## Track custom functions

LLM applications often have additional logic, such as pre-processing and post-processing, prompts, and more, that you want to track. Use this approach when you want Weave to capture your own functions alongside the LLM calls it traces automatically.

**Python**

Weave lets you manually track these Calls using the [`@weave.op`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/python-sdk#function-op) decorator. For example:

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave

# Initialize Weave Tracing
weave.init('intro-example')

# Call your function -- Weave will automatically track inputs and outputs
print(my_function("World"))
```

result.title: Verdict
result.heading: Getting started
result.text:
## Getting started

To enable Weave tracing for your Verdict pipelines, call `weave.init(project=...)` at the beginning of your script. Use the `project` argument to log to a specific Weights & Biases Team name with `team-name/project-name`, or pass `project-name` to log to your default team or entity.

```python lines {7} theme={"system"}
import weave
from verdict import Pipeline
from verdict.common.judge import JudgeUnit
from verdict.schema import Schema

# Initialize Weave with your project name
weave.init("verdict_demo")

# Create a simple evaluation pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline()
pipeline = pipeline >> JudgeUnit().prompt("Rate the quality of this text: {source.text}")

# Create sample data
data = Schema.of(text="This is a sample text for evaluation.")

# Run the pipeline - Weave traces this automatically
output = pipeline.run(data)

print(output)
```

# Verdict

> Use Verdict evaluation framework with Weave to trace and monitor your LLM evaluation pipelines

[GitHub source](https://github.com/wandb/examples/blob/master/weave/docs/quickstart_verdict.ipynb)

Weave is designed to track and log all calls made through the [Verdict Python library](https://verdict.haizelabs.com/docs/) automatically.

When working with AI evaluation pipelines, debugging matters. Whether a pipeline step fails, outputs are unexpected, or nested operations create confusion, pinpointing issues can be hard. Verdict applications often consist of multiple pipeline steps, judges, and transformations, so it helps to understand the inner workings of your evaluation workflows.

Weave streamlines this process by automatically capturing traces for your [Verdict](https://verdict.readthedocs.io/) applications. This lets you monitor and analyze your pipeline's performance to debug and optimize your AI evaluation workflows.

results.snippet:
## Manual Call tracking

If neither automatic integration nor the `weave.op` decorator fits your workflow, you can manually create Calls using the API directly. This approach gives you full control over when a Call starts and ends, at the cost of more boilerplate.

**Python**

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave

# Initialize Weave Tracing
client = weave.init('intro-example')

def my_function(name: str):
    # Start a Call
    call = client.create_call(op="my_function", inputs={"name": name})

    # ... your function code ...

    # End a Call
    client.finish_call(call, output="Hello, World!")

# Call your function
print(my_function("World"))
```

**TypeScript**

```text theme={"system"}
This feature is not available in the TypeScript SDK yet.
```

**HTTP API**

* Start a Call: [POST `/call/start`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/service-api/calls/call-start).
* End a Call: [POST `/call/end`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/service-api/calls/call-end).

`weave.init()` sets up Weave tracing for your Python process. It sends tracking information to a CoreWeave Forge team and project. The usual project string is `"your-team/your-project"` [S4].

**What it does**
- It tells Weave which team and project to log traces to. If that project doesn't exist in your team yet, Weave creates it [S4].
- After it runs, Weave automatically tracks calls to supported LLM libraries. To also capture the inputs, outputs and code of your own functions, add the `@weave.op()` decorator to them [S4].
- When a traced function runs, Weave prints links in the terminal where you can view the traces [S4].

**Which project string to pass**
- `"team-name/project-name"`: logs to that specific team (a team is the Forge group that owns projects) [S2, S4].
- `"project-name"`: logs to your default team [S2, S4].

**Before you start**
- You need a CoreWeave Forge account, Python 3.10 or newer, and `pip install weave`. The quickstart example also installs `openai` and needs an OpenAI API key set as an environment variable [S5].

import weave

# Replace the placeholders with your Forge team and project names
weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

@weave.op()
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

greet("World")  # Weave records this call's inputs and outputs
```
